transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-12
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE); Ethan Ruiz (CTO, SableForge), Priya Nair (Lead SRE), Alicia Gomez (ML Eng), Tom Brooks (Security)

Auto-generated summary (quick):
- Deep technical sync on artifact bundle transport, offline licensing, GPU driver compatibility, and runtime tuning for on-prem/air-gapped deployment.
- Focus on ensuring artifact signing, checksums, and an offline activation flow that matches SableForge security policy.
- Discussed KV cache warmup strategies, batching policies, and quantization tradeoffs to meet 100ms median token latency and target throughput.
- Agreed next steps: share runbook, confirm hardware/OS specs, schedule bench run.

Topics covered:
- Artifact distribution (transport media, checksums, signing)
- Offline license activation (tokens, expiry, renewals)
- GPU driver and CUDA compat matrix; kernel/OS caveats
- Runtime perf: KV cache, continuous batching, sequence-length tuning
- Quantization recommendations and off-line quant artifacts
- Security constraints: air-gap, HSM/KMS, audit logs

Action items (captured at top): Jordan to send runbook and hashes; Maya to prepare quant profiles; Priya to confirm hardware/OS.

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round robin, and then Maya will jump into the runtime notes. Um, Ethan, Priya, thanks for making time.
[00:00:18] Ethan: Yeah thanks Jordan. We, we wanted to get into the specifics — we are planning a fully air-gapped install in our DC and need to make sure the bundle transport and offline license steps are rock solid.
[00:00:30] Maya: Cool. I'll start with an overview of the bundle. So the on-prem artifact is a signed tarball, it contains the model artifacts, the runtime container image (OCI tar), the license blob and a manifest. We sign the tar with our internal GPG key and include an accompanying SHA256 and a detached signature.
[00:00:52] Tom (Security): You said GPG, do you support enterprise PKI or do we need to accept a Redwood-signed key?
[00:01:00] Jordan: Short answer: both. We can accept your PKI-signed certs — the runbook has a step for adding an enterprise CA to the verification chain. If needed we can also do a cross-signed approach.
[00:01:12] Priya: For transport, we have strict physical media rules. We'll probably use encrypted SSDs, ship via our courier partners. What's the recommended checksum/verification flow so our ops team can validate before touching the air-gapped cluster?
[00:01:26] Maya: Recommended: we provide three artifacts — the tarball, a SHA256/sha512 sum file, and a GPG detached signature. Ops validates the checksum, then verifies signature against the provided cert. We also support an additional HMAC file for a second layer. We include instructions for using 'gpg --verify' in the runbook.
[00:01:46] Alicia: A nit — sometimes filenames get mangled by SFTP tools. Can you put a manifest with file sizes and creation timestamps? That helps our automation.
[00:01:56] Luis (Redwood SE): Yes, the manifest contains file names, sizes, timestamps, and a UUID for the bundle. It also lists model ids and quant profile version.
[00:02:08] [crosstalk] Ethan: Great. About licensing — do you use online activation? We need an offline flow.
[00:02:15] Maya: For air-gapped installs we issue a signed license blob in the bundle. The blob contains a license id, allowed model ids, cluster fingerprint, and expiry. Activation is local: the runtime calls the local license manager which validates the signature against our public key. No outbound call is necessary for activation.
[00:02:32] Tom: How do renewals work if we have expiry and no outbound network?
[00:02:36] Jordan: Two options: one, you schedule periodic exchange windows where you send a CSR-like request file out via courier and we return a renewal license; two, for long-term deployments we provide a long-duration license and an offline license updater script you run when you get a fresh signed blob. We'll document both in the runbook.
[00:02:54] Priya: Is there a way to rotate keys locally? Our policy requires annual key rotation and HSM integration.
[00:03:01] Maya: Yes. We support storing the private key in a customer HSM; the runtime can be configured to use PKCS#11 to validate and sign locally. For rotation, you swap the certs and we provide a small verification tool to ensure chain validity.
[00:03:14] Ethan: Okay good. Now on the GPU side: our cluster has a mix of A10Gs and A5000s, some nodes are on RHEL8 with 5.14 kernel. Any known driver/kernel issues?
[00:03:28] Luis: We published a compat matrix in the doc bundle; short version — for A10G and A5000 we recommend NVIDIA driver 530.x or newer and CUDA 12.1 for best perf. RHEL8/5.14 can work but we've seen issues with older kernel modules where the NVIDIA module doesn't persist across kpatches. We'll include the tested OS kernel versions in the runbook.
[00:03:47] Priya: What about MIG/partitioning? We plan to use full GPUs but may explore MPS later.
[00:03:53] Maya: Our runtime prefers dedicated GPU contexts for the low latency SLOs. MIG is supported on A100; for A10/A5000 MPS can help throughput but it can increase tail latency. We'll show numbers in the bench plan.
[00:04:07] Ethan: Benchmarks. We need to hit roughly 100ms median for 1-token latency at steady state and 8k tokens/sec total throughput across the pool for a mixed mix of 2048 and 512 seq lengths.
[00:04:20] Maya: Okay, a couple notes: first-token latency is dominated by KV cache miss and model sharding. We recommend a warm-up phase where you pre-warm the KV cache with a representative prompt set. Second, continuous batching settings — you can tune max batch size and max latency for pooling. We'll provide a default policy that targets 90ms median at typical seq length 512; with quantization to int8 and our kernel toggles you should hit 100ms for 2048 too but that depends on GPU memory.
[00:04:48] Alicia: You mentioned KV cache warmup. Practically how do we do that in an air-gapped set?
[00:04:53] Maya: We provide a warmup script that replays a canonical corpus of prompts from the bundle against the local model to populate KV caches. Script runs as a preflight after install; it accepts a target requests-per-second and duration. For large pools we support distributed warm-up where each node warms a shard subset to reduce overall time.
[00:05:11] Priya: Does the warm-up script need internet?
[00:05:14] Maya: No. Everything is local, the corpus is in the bundle. It's deterministic so you can re-run it any time.
[00:05:19] [pause, rustling]
[00:05:25] Ethan: Quantization — do you support 4-bit, 8-bit and is there an automatic pipeline to produce quant artifacts?
[00:05:31] Maya: We ship pre-quantized variants for popular open models when available, and we support an offline quantization tool in the bundle that runs on a dedicated worker node. The tool supports symmetric/asymmetric int8 and 4-bit per-channel, and we provide recommended presets. Note quan-tization can change output probabilities slightly; we include eval prompts so you can run a local quality check.
[00:05:53] Luis: Important: 4-bit paths may require kernel-level fused ops that are CUDA-version-sensitive. We'll include a mapping of quant profile -> required driver and CuDNN.
[00:06:05] Alicia: Any advice on mixing quantized and fp16 models in the same pool?
[00:06:09] Maya: It's supported. We recommend routing lower-priority traffic to quantized models and keeping fp16 for zero-shot/high-quality paths. Our smart routing can fallback automatically when capacity is constrained.
[00:06:20] Priya: Can we do a canary rollout on-prem? Like deploy to five nodes, run benchmarks, then expand?
[00:06:25] Jordan: Yes. The private control plane allows you to pin versions per-rack. For fully air-gapped you still get a local control plane that supports canary and rollbacks via the manifest. We'll include CLI commands in the runbook.
[00:06:35] Tom: Audit logs — we need immutable logs for who activated what and when. Is there a way to export signed audit events?
[00:06:41] Maya: The runtime writes signed audit events to a local secure log. We support a log exporter that creates a signed bundle with timestamps. If you have an HSM we can sign per-event.
[00:06:51] Ethan: Great. Back to drivers — what about driver packaging? We're constrained on allowed packages. Can you supply a driver tar with kernel module pre-built for our kernel?
[00:07:01] Luis: We can provide a driver bundle: pre-built kernel module for common kernels and a source fallback with build instructions for unusual kernels. The runbook includes a checksum and signature for the driver bundle. For RHEL8 we recommend the pre-built we tested.
[00:07:14] Priya: If we build from source, do you support out-of-tree module rebuilding steps?
[00:07:18] Maya: Yes, we include dkms-style scripts and a module build helper in the bundle. We tested it on RHEL and Ubuntu kernels listed in the compat matrix.
[00:07:27] Alicia: There's sometimes friction around kernel headers and internal packaging policies, we'd like a dry-run script to verify prerequisites before attempt.
[00:07:33] Jordan: We'll add a preflight checklist script that validates headers, kernel version, and available disk/ram on nodes.
[00:07:40] [10 minute mark summary by Jordan: confirm runbook, manifest, and preflight scripts will be included]
[00:07:55] Ethan: On perf numbers: can you share a sample run that demonstrates your warmup + batching hitting our target?
[00:08:02] Maya: I'll summarize — in our internal perf lab on an A10G with CUDA12.1 and driver 530.41 we saw median 1-token latency ~85ms with int8 quant on a 7B model at steady-state after warmup, and sustained throughput ~3k tokens/sec per GPU under continuous batching. With four GPUs in a pool and the right routing we can get to your 8k target. But sequence distribution matters; longer seqs reduce effective throughput.
[00:08:27] Ethan: Are those numbers with KV cache fully warm?
[00:08:30] Maya: Correct. Cold start first-token latencies were 320ms in that run before warmup.
[00:08:35] Priya: Can you give visibility on memory footprint for int8 vs fp16?
[00:08:39] Luis: int8 reduced model footprint by ~45% in our tests compared to fp16; that allows larger batch sizes or more concurrent streams per GPU. We'll include a table in the runbook showing memory vs perf.
[00:08:51] Tom: Anything about telemetry? We need limited telemetry only — no payloads.
[00:08:56] Jordan: For private installs telemetry is opt-in. By default we collect anonymized metrics about latency, token counts, and error rates. Customers can disable telemetry entirely; we provide a diagnostic bundle you can upload manually for support.
[00:09:09] Alicia: For the warm-up corpus, can we add our proprietary prompts?
[00:09:13] Maya: Yes, the warmup script accepts a custom corpus and you can sign it locally. That will yield a KV cache aligned to your traffic.
[00:09:21] [switching to bench plan specifics]
[00:09:25] Maya: Proposed bench plan: 1) baseline cold start test, 2) KV warmup with our corpus at 500 rps for 10 minutes, 3) ramp to target throughput over 15 minutes, 4) soak at target for 30 minutes, capture p50/p95/p99 and GPU metrics. We'll send a bench harness and a sample k6 script.
[00:09:45] Priya: For the bench harness, do we need to instrument inner metrics? We want to correlate GPU SM/utilization with latency.
[00:09:50] Luis: The bench harness exports GPU metrics via nvidia-smi and DCGM; we also have trace hooks to emit per-request timing to the local tracing collector.
[00:09:59] Ethan: What about KV cache eviction policies?
[00:10:03] Maya: We default to LRU-ish shard-aware eviction with configurable limits per-model. For long-tail workloads we recommend a larger cache size or a pinned prefix cache for common prompts. Cache size is configurable in the runtime config.
[00:10:16] Alicia: Any recommended defaults for mixed seq lengths?
[00:10:19] Maya: Use dynamic batching with max_batch 64 and max_wait 12ms to balance latency/throughput. For 2048-heavy workloads you may reduce max_batch but increase concurrency. We'll provide presets.
[00:10:33] [00:10:40] Tom: Security question — how do you ensure the bundle hasn't been tampered with after shipment?
[00:10:44] Jordan: The runbook includes step-by-step verification: compare SHA512, verify signature against customer-trusted cert, and validate bundle UUID against an out-of-band email. We can also include a secondary OTP code printed on the manifest as an additional confirmation.
[00:10:58] Priya: Sizing question — how many GPUs would you recommend to meet the 8k tokens/sec target for our mix?
[00:11:03] Maya: Rough estimate: with int8 quant on 7B models we expect ~3k tokens/sec per A10G, so 3 GPUs is a safe start, 4 for headroom. For 13B models you'd need about 2x the GPUs. We'll give a sizing table.
[00:11:16] Ethan: If we later switch to different cards, how disruptive is re-quantization?
[00:11:20] Luis: Re-quant requires regenerating the quant artifacts; it can be done offline and pushed as a separate bundle. Runtime can run mixed artifacts during a rolling upgrade.
[00:11:29] Priya: About the offline license blob — can we integrate it with our internal license server so we don't have to hand-carry renewals?
[00:11:35] Maya: Yes, we can provide an API contract for your license server to create signed license blobs using your key; then Redwood only validates signature and model ids. We'll include the spec.
[00:11:47] Tom: Any gotchas with time drift? Our nodes are isolated and NTP is disabled for compliance.
[00:11:52] Jordan: The license validator supports a grace window and accepts an explicit signed timestamp in the blob. If you can't use NTP we recommend including a signed attestation from your admin with the local time range. We'll document the process.
[00:12:05] [mid-call recap from Jordan: runbook, bench plan, driver bundles, warmup scripts, license renewal paths]
[00:12:20] Ethan: Small operational question — disk layout and tmpfs usage for kv caches?
[00:12:25] Maya: KV caches are in-memory; however we keep an optional local snapshot on disk to speed up restarts. The snapshot is compressed and the path is configurable. We recommend tmpfs for shards if nodes have abundant RAM to reduce I/O.
[00:12:38] Priya: Does snapshotting conflict with our disk encryption requirements?
[00:12:41] Luis: Snapshot files can be stored on encrypted volumes; the runbook shows where to configure the path. The snapshot is also encrypted at rest using a local key.
[00:12:51] Alicia: Any specific kernel tunables you recommend for JVM-like limits? (laughs)
[00:12:55] Maya: (laughs) Mostly the usual: increase file descriptors, tune swappiness to 1, and make sure THP (transparent huge pages) is off for some memory alloc patterns. We'll list the sysctl changes.
[00:13:06] Ethan: Do you have a suggested maintenance window length for the first rollout?
[00:13:10] Jordan: We recommend a 6-hour window for install + warmup + benching. Usually install takes ~60–90 minutes, warmup scales with corpus size but with distributed warmup you should be fine in ~60–90 min, then benching 90 min to collect steady-state metrics.
[00:13:26] Priya: Any sample CLI commands for rolling back if an install fails?
[00:13:30] Luis: Yes: 'redwoodctl rollback --manifest <id> --nodes <selector>' We'll include examples. The local control plane also has a dry-run verify command.
[00:13:39] [silence briefly as people take notes]
[00:13:45] Jordan: Ok next — packaging and signing. We can support either a single monolithic tar or split bundles per model. Which do you prefer?
[00:13:52] Ethan: We prefer split bundles per model so we can stage updates model-by-model.
[00:13:56] Maya: Fine. We'll create a per-model tar with a common runtime patch and a small delta mechanism to reduce transfer size.
[00:14:05] Alicia: Are deltas binary diffs? We need a robust apply that won't leave nodes in half-upgraded state.
[00:14:10] Luis: Deltas are signed binary patches. The apply has a transactional two-phase commit: stage -> verify -> switch. If verify fails it rollbacks to previous files.
[00:14:21] Tom: On auditability, can each stage log the operator who applied the patch?
[00:14:25] Maya: Yes, we capture operator identity and sign the transition event.
[00:14:30] [closing 10 minutes: clarify next steps and responsibilities]
[00:14:32] Jordan: To recap and action owners: Jordan will send runbook, driver bundles, and sample bench harness. Maya will attach quant profiles and warmup scripts. Priya will confirm hardware/OS and maintenance window. Tom will review the license rotation HSM plan. Any other asks?
[00:14:47] Ethan: Please include a short checklist for our procurement team for the courier manifest.
[00:14:51] Jordan: Will do, we'll include shipping manifest template.
[00:14:55] Alicia: Also include a minimal troubleshooting FAQ for common driver build failures.
[00:14:58] Luis: Noted, will include.
[00:15:02] [end of formal notes — informal wrap; some small talk] 
[00:15:10] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of transcript.
